1.pericope_label: The rod turned into a serpent

schools.summary: Calvin attributes the hesitation to timidity rather than stubbornness and finds the same conflict in every believer, contrasts the contemptible crook with the terror it would inspire, reads the flight as God frightening His servant so that he might judge what Pharaoh would feel, and distinguishes miracles that prepare faith from those that confirm it; Gill explains the seizing of the tail and insists the sign was for Israel and not for Moses.

Henry reads the objection as meaning only that some might not believe at first, since a flat contradiction of God’s promise could not be justified, and draws from Moses’s reluctance that God clothes with humility those He designs for service.

Clarke takes the rod for a shepherd’s crook, notes that the Hebrew names no species of serpent, and draws the moral that implicit obedience conquers all difficulties; Wesley joins him in supplying the words missing from the unfinished sentence.

Ellicott denies that the opening word can mean "perhaps" and holds that Moses expressed a settled conviction, explains the fear by four centuries without any appearance of God, generalises that miracles cluster at crises and cease between them, argues from etymology for a common walking-stick rather than a shepherd’s crook, and takes the verse as sanctioning the evidential purpose of miracles; Keil and Delitzsch make the crook the sign of the calling laid down and the serpent the power prevailing in Egypt.

debates: Whether Moses said the people would not believe or only that they might not, Henry softening the objection and Ellicott refusing the softening on the ground that the word never means "perhaps".
What the rod was: a shepherd’s crook (Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Calvin) or an ordinary walking-stick (Ellicott, from the etymology).
Whose faith the sign was meant to serve, Gill excluding Moses because the burning bush had already convinced him, while Calvin finds it strengthening Moses and compelling Israel at once.
outliers: Ellicott advances a general account of miracles as clustering at crises in God’s dealings and ceasing entirely between them.
Gill reports a comment that Moses was told to take the serpent by the tail because its head belonged not to him but to Christ, who was speaking from the bush.

6.pericope_label: The leprous hand and the water turned to blood

schools.summary: Calvin takes the sign as teaching that vigour withers and dryness revives at God’s word, applies it to Moses’s own exile and restoration, reads the accumulation of signs as divine longsuffering toward dullness, and holds that the third foretold the turning of Egypt’s own strongholds against her; Gill notes the signs were actually repeated before the people in Egypt.

Clarke describes the disease and its supposed incurability, argues that the instantaneous infliction and cure was chosen simply as an undeniable demonstration of divine power, and says no other reason need be sought; Wesley reads it as a sign that Moses would bring and remove diseases in Egypt and that leprous Israel would be cleansed in his bosom.

Ellicott identifies the white leprosy from Greek medical writers, suggests the Egyptians’ name for the Israelites may derive from Moses’s leprous hand, insists that the voice belongs to the sign itself rather than to Moses, explains the ascending order of the three signs as patience with reasonable doubt, and reads all three as significant of Moses’s mission; Keil and Delitzsch make the third a demonstration of power over the might and gods of Egypt.

debates: Whether the leprous sign carries any meaning beyond its evidential force, which Clarke expressly denies while Calvin, Wesley and Ellicott each propose a different significance.
Whose voice the "voice of the sign" is, Ellicott rejecting the reading that makes it the voice of Moses attested by the miracle.
outliers: Ellicott suggests that the Egyptian writers’ name for the Israelites may go back to Moses displaying a leprous hand.
Calvin reads Moses’s forty years in Midian as itself a kind of leprosy, from which the sign promised restoration.

10.pericope_label: I am not eloquent: the objection from slow speech

schools.summary: Gill grounds the answer in the God who gave the faculty of speech; Calvin distinguishes the modesty of confessing a defect from the injustice of asking to be discharged, allows fear that does not overcome obedience, and argues from the government of the tongue that eloquence is a matter of special grace which God can give or take at will.

Henry describes Moses as a great philosopher and no orator, argues that men are not to be judged by fluency since much wisdom hides behind a slow tongue, and holds that God chooses messengers with the fewest natural advantages so that His grace may appear the more.

Clarke confronts Stephen’s description of Moses as mighty in words and offers three solutions, including an imperfect command of Hebrew after eighty years abroad, and warns that He who made the eye and ear also made the blind and deaf; Wesley gives the character of Moses in the same terms as Henry.

Keil and Delitzsch deny that the defect was stammering and take it for an absence of the gift of speech, and observe that when the objections were exhausted the true reason appeared; Ellicott passes on the tradition that Moses could not pronounce the labials, explains the idiom for past time, and corrects the tense of the question about the mouth.

debates: What Moses’s impediment actually was: a real difficulty of mouth and tongue but not stammering (Keil and Delitzsch), an inability to sound the labials (the tradition Ellicott reports), or an imperfect command of Hebrew (Clarke).
How the description of Moses as mighty in words is to be squared with this verse, which Clarke answers three ways and Henry and Wesley by distinguishing weight of matter from fluency of delivery.
outliers: Wesley reproduces Henry’s characterisation of Moses almost word for word, including the same two proof texts.
Calvin argues that God deliberately employs the least suitable instruments so that His own power may be the more evident, reaching independently the conclusion Henry draws from the apostles.

13.pericope_label: Send by whom thou wilt: the anger of the Lord and the gift of Aaron

schools.summary: Calvin rejects the christological reading as forced and contradicted by God’s anger, prefers the sense of sending anyone at all, treats the verse as proof that obedience is the best sacrifice, judges that Aaron was conceded to Moses’s diffidence with part of his honour, and finds in the elder brother’s subordination a witness that gifts are distributed at God’s pleasure; Gill lists four possible expressions of the divine anger and credits Moses with recording his own weakness.

Clarke reports the messianic reading of the request and rejects it as pressing a passage with no obvious tendency that way, dismisses as fanciful the argument that Aaron’s appointment explains why Christ could not yet come, and derives the thyrsus of Bacchus and the caduceus of Mercury from the rod of Moses; Wesley holds that self-distrust which clogs us in duty displeases God, that the best gifts fail without grace, and that the shepherd’s crook kept Moses from being ashamed of his origins.

Ellicott renders the request as curt and scarcely reverent, argues that "the Levite" is a title of honour rather than a distinguishing mark, and insists Moses kept the higher place since God spoke to Aaron only through him; Keil and Delitzsch reconcile Aaron’s setting out with the later command that he go.

debates: Whether "send by the hand of him whom thou wilt send" asks for the Messiah, which Clarke and Calvin independently reject on the same ground, that God would not have been angry at such a prayer.
What tone the request carries, Ellicott calling it impatient and scarcely reverent while Gill reads the opening words as accepting the blame or the burden.
Whether Aaron had been appointed from the first or was granted in concession to Moses’s weakness, Calvin weighing both and preferring the second.
outliers: Gill cannot determine how the divine anger was expressed and sets out four possibilities without choosing.
Clarke argues at length that the classical myths of Bacchus and Mercury are borrowings from the life and rod of Moses.

18.pericope_label: Leave from Jethro and the return to Egypt

schools.summary: Calvin thinks Moses dared not speak of a call so incredible that he would be taken for a liar, turns Jethro’s consent into a lesson on the value of a long-proved reputation, holds that the verse is inserted out of its chronological place, and contrasts the poverty of the ass with the sufficiency of the rod; Gill takes the removal of the family as proof that Moses expected to stay.

Henry holds that communion with God does not excuse a man from the duties of his calling, attributes the silence about the vision to reticence, and suspects that a secret fear of his old enemies lay under all Moses’s stated objections.

Clarke rejects modesty as the explanation and substitutes prudence, since the news might have reached Egypt first and raised the country against him, and treats the addition in the Greek and Coptic as a marginal gloss; Wesley calls the word in Midian a second vision.

Ellicott holds the stated reason true though not the chief one and defends Moses’s right to withhold the rest, explains the tribal obligation to ask leave, draws a portrait of Jethro as a second Melchizedek, and calls the rod of God an emphatic title; Keil and Delitzsch refuse both the pluperfect reading and the source-critical one, and set the poor appearance of Moses against the staff he carried.

debates: Why Moses concealed his commission from Jethro: reticence about divine favours (Henry), political prudence (Clarke, who names and rejects the modesty explanation), fear of not being believed (Calvin), or a legitimate statement of one true motive among several (Ellicott).
Whether the word spoken in Midian is recorded out of its chronological order, which Calvin affirms and Keil and Delitzsch expressly deny along with the suggestion that it comes from another hand.
Whether one ass or several carried the family, Clarke following the Greek plural and Ellicott allowing the singular to stand for the kind.
outliers: Calvin argues that the poor are driven to crime more by shame than by hunger, and counts Moses’s willingness to appear openly poor a heavy temptation withstood.
Ellicott insists that a man may state one of his motives and withhold the others without fault.

21.pericope_label: I will harden his heart, and Israel my firstborn son

schools.summary: Calvin holds that whatever opposed the deliverance arose from God’s own secret counsel and that Pharaoh was hardened so as to be the more gloriously overwhelmed, reads the sonship as the legal answer to Pharaoh’s otherwise lawful claim while refusing to extend it into a general exemption of believers from earthly rule, and places the threat at the end of the embassy; Gill takes the saying as a command of right.

Clarke reports the controversy, cites Augustine that God hardens by withholding mercy rather than by infusing malice, and argues from the Hebrew verb that it means to strengthen or embolden; Wesley makes God permit Satan to harden the heart at last, and reads the title of son as meaning simply that Israel is dear and honourable.

Ellicott distinguishes three periods in which the heart hardens itself, Pharaoh hardens it, and God hardens it as a judgment after two refusals, denies that the sonship of Israel is a metaphor, and places the threat against Pharaoh’s firstborn immediately before the tenth plague; Keil and Delitzsch define the word for wonder, take the whole series as given potentially with the staff, and ground Israel’s sonship in election from the call of Abraham.

debates: How Pharaoh’s heart is hardened: by God withholding mercy already despised (Clarke, citing Augustine), by a sequence in which the heart, then Pharaoh, then God act in turn (Ellicott), by God permitting Satan at the last (Wesley), or by God’s own secret counsel from the outset (Calvin).
Whether Israel’s sonship is a figure for tender regard, as Clarke and Wesley take it, or a real adoption, as Ellicott insists against them.
outliers: Calvin restricts the political force of the argument, denying that the exemption of Israel implies any general release of believers from subjection to kings.
Clarke observes that the Hebrew verb for hardening ordinarily means to strengthen or embolden, and is written at the end of most biblical books to hearten the reader.

24.pericope_label: The Lord met him at the inn, and Zipporah circumcised her son

schools.summary: Gill identifies Moses rather than the child as the one threatened and rejects the alternative accounts of the offence; Calvin refuses to say in what form God met him, rebukes those who pronounce it a disease and those who blame the taking of the family, and holds that the irregular circumcision was accepted by indulgence rather than absolutely, warning that this is no precedent for hypocrites.

Henry traces the neglect to an unequal marriage and to the cooling of zeal in long isolation from the faithful, and lays down that omissions are sins, the neglect of the covenant seals implying that a man neither likes his bargain nor means to keep it.

Clarke reads the threatened firstborn as Gershom and reconstructs the whole passage accordingly, with the foreskin touching the feet of the Lord who had appeared in bodily form; Wesley repeats Henry’s account of the sin and judges Zipporah’s reproach unreasonable, approving the sending home of the family.

Ellicott identifies the visitation as a fatal illness, denies that there was any inn in that country, explains the stone knife from Egyptian and Israelite usage, reads the casting down as a petulant reproach against a religion she thought barbarous, and takes the plural "bloods" of the two circumcisions; Keil and Delitzsch make the episode the lesson that Moses must prove faithful in his own house before executing his commission.

debates: Whether the life threatened was Moses’s, as Gill argues expressly against the alternative, or the uncircumcised son’s, as Clarke maintains at length.
What form the visitation took: a fatal illness (Ellicott), or something not to be determined, Calvin calling it too bold to name a disease.
What Zipporah meant by casting the foreskin down and by calling Moses a husband of bloods, Ellicott reading petulant reproach and Ellicott and Gill dividing over whose feet are meant.
outliers: Calvin holds that a rite performed rashly and irregularly was nonetheless accepted, but forbids drawing from it any general assurance for hypocrites.
Ellicott and Wesley agree that Zipporah and the children were sent back to Jethro at this point.

27.pericope_label: Aaron meets Moses, and the elders and people believe

schools.summary: Calvin observes that God says nothing of the deliverance and simply makes the elder brother the disciple of the younger, and infers that even an organ of the Spirit must hear God’s word from a man; he asks why the message was not given to Aaron directly and answers that the circuit was a test of faith; and he warns that the people’s belief had no living root and was scattered by the first adverse wind. Gill takes their response at face value as adoration and readiness to obey.

Clarke suggests a secret impulse or angelic ministry directed Aaron, notes that both arrived at the mountain together, thinks Aaron the better Hebrew speaker, and turns the people’s bowing into an argument that worship performed at perfect ease shows no sense of God’s majesty; Wesley draws from the brothers’ conference the rule that fellow servants in one work should understand one another fully.

Ellicott holds that Aaron’s directions must have been fuller or supplemented on the way, describes the surviving Israelite organisation under the elders whom Moses could invite but not convoke, finds the closing narrative much compressed, and refers the worship to the Lord rather than to Moses.

debates: Whether the people’s faith here was genuine, which Gill and Clarke assume and Calvin denies, calling it a mere assent that the first temptation dissipated.
Who was worshipped at the close, Ellicott reporting the view that Moses was the object and preferring the Lord.
Why the message passed through Moses to Aaron and only then to the people, Calvin treating the indirection as deliberate and Clarke explaining it by Aaron’s better command of Hebrew.
outliers: Calvin argues that a man who refuses to be taught through a human voice is unworthy to have God for his teacher.
Ellicott reconstructs an unrecorded second assembly, held after working hours, at which the people were shown the signs.
